system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2157-09-17 04:41:00 to 2157-09-18 15:09:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for uncontrolled type I diabetes with hyperglycemia and ketonuria, consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis, following a viral illness with high fevers and oral herpes. She had no anion gap and stable vital signs, with normal lipase ruling out acute pancreatitis. Her blood glucose improved with continuation of home insulin therapy. Fevers resolved without identified bacterial source, and flu testing was negative. Chronic abdominal pain was managed with transition to oral Dilaudid, and she tolerated oral intake. Per narcotics agreement, no hospital prescriptions were issued. She was discharged with stable glucose levels, instructions to continue home insulin, and follow-up with her primary care provider for pain and oral lesions.
problems: Diabetes with ketoacidosis, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ female with right upper quadrant pain.

COMPARISON:  CT available from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

FINDINGS:  This examination was limited due to difficulty with patient
positioning and breath-hold.  The liver is slightly echogenic.  No
intrahepatic bile duct dilation or focal lesion is detected.  The main portal
vein is patent, demonstrating proper hepatopetal flow.  The patient is status
post cholecystectomy.  No neighboring focal fluid collections are seen.  The
CBD was not visualized due to patient motion.  No ascites is present.

IMPRESSION:  
1. Limited study due to difficulty with patient positioning.  Otherwise, no
acute process seen.
2. Echogenic liver, reflecting fatty infiltration. More advanced disease such
as fibrosis cannot be excluded with this technique.

diagnoses.long_title: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling really off—tired, achy, and my stomach hurts more than usual. It’s on the right side now, not the left like normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a few days. I also had a cough and burning when I pee. My doctor gave me Cipro for a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about your blood sugar? I see it was very high in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was over 600. I used 30 units of Humalog and it didn’t budge. I turned my insulin pump off yesterday when I changed the site… I forgot to turn it back on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain the high sugar. We gave you insulin and fluids through an IV. Your levels are coming down now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also felt burning and swelling after taking my meds—Cipro, Neurontin, and cough syrup. I went to urgent care and got Benadryl.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a possible reaction. We’ve stopped the Cipro for now. The urine culture showed contamination, so no active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried it was a bad infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not seeing signs of that. Your lungs are clear, and the cough is likely from congestion. No fever now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my stomach pain? It’s different this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound. It was hard to get good images because of positioning, but we didn’t see gallstones or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes were a bit high, but they’re improving. It could be related to your chronic pancreatitis. The pain pattern has changed, so we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had pancreatitis before. My doctors wanted to do an MRCP with secretin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we tried to schedule that while you were here, but anesthesia wasn’t available. You mentioned you’d prefer to do it outpatient?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want to stay longer than I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. Your PCP and gastroenterologist will coordinate it. For now, we’re managing your pain with Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your glucose is 252—much better. Sodium is normalizing too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting you on a regular diabetic diet. We’ve increased your Lantus insulin to 30 units at night as your intake improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually use my insulin pump between meals. Should I start that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your endocrinologist recommends stopping the pump. It’s not part of your official regimen and may have contributed to the high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it helps me control spikes after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but without proper oversight, it can be risky. We’ll stick to your prescribed sliding scale with Humalog for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are trending down—ALT and AST are lower. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fatty liver from my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The ultrasound showed echogenic liver, which often means fatty infiltration. We can’t rule out fibrosis, but it’s not acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having chest tightness. Is that from the asthma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG showed sinus tachycardia, but no new changes. The tightness was pleuritic—likely from coughing. It’s improved, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a little. I’m still using my inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using them as prescribed. We’ll continue monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your glucose is stable, and your pain is better. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? What about the lung nodules from my old CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re likely inflammatory, but we recommend a follow-up chest CT in three months to check them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’m on a contract with my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with your usual Dilaudid prescription. No new narcotics were given here, per your agreement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your primary doctor. She’ll help schedule the MRCP and review your insulin plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure to keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re doing much better—glucose under control, pain improved, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot clearer than when I came in. Thanks for helping me get back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call your doctor if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with abdominal pain and critically high blood glucose, found to be due to insulin pump discontinuation and possible infection. She had a history of chronic pancreatitis and gastroparesis, with new right-sided abdominal pain. Initial concerns for biliary obstruction were ruled out by a limited RUQ ultrasound showing no acute process, though fatty liver was noted. Hyperglycemia resolved with IV insulin and transition to scheduled Lantus, with discontinuation of the non-prescribed insulin pump. Pain was managed with home Dilaudid regimen per narcotics agreement. Urine culture showed contamination, and antibiotics were discontinued. Chest tightness improved without intervention. The patient declined inpatient MRCP with secretin and will follow up as an outpatient. She was discharged home in stable condition, tolerating diet, with plans for chest CT follow-up in three months.
